summary: OpenID is widely used for web single sign-on, while SASL and GSS-API are frameworks that applications use for authentication. This RFC defines a mechanism for both so existing OpenID Identity Providers can be used by applications that speak SASL or GSS-API.

plainLanguage.summary: You already have a library card from one place. This lets other clubs accept that card instead of making you a new one.

questions: how to use openid with sasl

how does openid work with imap
subtitle: How a mail client can log in with an OpenID by handing the web part of the login to a browser.

tldr.problem: OpenID was built for web pages, but mail, chat and other protocols log in through SASL or GSS-API, so they could not use existing OpenID Identity Providers.
tldr.mechanism: A new SASL mechanism named OPENID20 carries the user's OpenID to the server. The server answers with a URL, the client opens it in a browser for the real login, and the client sends back a bare "=" while it waits for the result.
tldr.outcome: Existing OpenID Providers work unchanged, and only the Relying Party and the client need new code. The mechanism must run over TLS, offers no security layer of its own and does not support channel binding.

today: RFC 6616 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2012, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines OPENID20 for OpenID 2.0 only.

sections.title: Why OpenID Meets SASL
sections.content:
OpenID 2.0 is a web-based, three-party protocol. A user offers identity assertions to a web server, called the Relying Party (RP), with the help of an identity provider, called the OpenID Provider (OP). Its purpose is to verify that an end user controls an identifier.

SASL is used by application protocols such as IMAP, POP and XMPP to keep authentication modular, so newer mechanisms can be added. The GSS-API gives applications one interface to several authentication mechanisms. RFC 6616 defines a pure SASL mechanism for OpenID that also conforms to GS2, the bridge between SASL and GSS-API, so it is a GSS-API mechanism too.

The design reuses OpenID as far as possible. It adds no authentication, integrity or confidentiality layer of its own and expects existing layers such as TLS to stay in use. Most of the exchange happens in a normal web browser, so the specification is only appropriate when such a browser is available. Changes are needed in the Relying Party and the client. No change to the OpenID Provider is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Some programs already know one way to check who you are, and websites know another. This document makes a translator so the programs can use the website way.

sections.title: The Eleven-Step Login Flow
sections.content:
The SASL server plays the Relying Party. Because OpenID Providers must not change, an analogous flow was built around the SASL session, which already exists as a connection between client and server. The steps are:

  • The server advertises the mechanism, and the client starts authentication by sending the User-Supplied Identifier. The mechanism is client-first.
  • The RP normalizes the identifier, performs discovery to find the OP Endpoint URL, and optionally sets up an association, a shared secret established with Diffie-Hellman key exchange that lets messages be checked with an HMAC.
  • The RP builds an authentication request as a URI, because OpenID's own indirect methods (HTTP redirects and HTML form submission) do not fit SASL. The client sends back a response of just =.
  • The client builds a URL from the request and gives it to the OP through a browser or other handler. The user authenticates there and approves or declines. This step is outside SASL.
  • The OP sends the result back to the RP indirectly through the client, over HTTP and TLS. If no association exists, the RP MAY send a check_authentication request directly to the OP.
  • The SASL server finishes with an outcome, optionally carrying Simple Registration (SREG) attributes.

The client MUST send the = response. After processing the redirect it waits for the final SASL decision while OpenID continues in the browser. The RFC explains that a signal from the browser to the SASL client would raise a substantial inter-process communication problem, so authentication is externalized to the browser instead.
sections.plainLanguage: You tell the club your library card number. The club sends you to the library desk to show the card, and you come back and say you are done. Then the club lets you in.

sections.title: The OPENID20 SASL Mechanism
sections.content:
The mechanism is named OPENID20. It can transfer an authorization identity through the gs2-header, and it offers no security layer. It has four messages:

  • Initial response from the client: the GS2 header followed by the OpenID identifier as a URI. The gs2-nonstd-flag MUST NOT be present, and the gs2-cb-flag MUST be n, because channel binding is not supported. Extensible Resource Identifiers (XRIs) MUST NOT be used.
  • Authentication request from the server: a URL whose openid.mode is either checkid_immediate or checkid_setup. The server MUST append a unique transaction ID to the return_to part, and it SHOULD be large enough to resist guessing.
  • A fixed = from the client.
  • Outcome data from the server on success, which MAY carry SREG attributes.

SREG attributes are encoded by stripping openid.sreg. from each name and writing the results as URI-style parameters, for example email=lear@example.com&fullname=Eliot%20Lear. A client that does not support SREG MUST ignore them, and a client MUST ignore unknown attributes.

Section 2.1 adds that OpenID has no transaction IDs of its own, so the RP MUST encode a nonce or transaction ID in the URIs it sends through the client, as a base URI or fragment of return_to. The nonce MUST be at least 2^32 bits and large enough for well beyond the number of concurrent transactions the server sees.
sections.plainLanguage: The conversation has four short turns: your card number, a link to follow, the word "done", and the answer. Each link carries a ticket number so the club knows which visitor is which.

sections.title: Failures and Error Reporting
sections.content:
RFC 4422 forbids extra information in an unsuccessful authentication outcome. So when authentication fails, openid.error and openid.error_code are sent as an additional challenge instead. The protocol is in lockstep, so the client answers with one more exchange containing =, and then the server sends an application-level outcome.

The failure form of the outcome data starts with openid.error followed by = and a value. The mechanism must also run only over channels protected by TLS, and the client MUST validate the server certificate.
sections.plainLanguage: If you are turned away, the club first tells you why in a note, waits for you to say "ok", and then officially says no.

sections.title: The GSS-API Mechanism
sections.content:
The same mechanism is a GSS-API mechanism. The OpenID user is the GSS-API Initiator and the Relying Party is the Acceptor. The OpenID Provider has no GSS-API role. The messages are the same, except that the GS2 header and channel binding data are left out, and the initial context token header from RFC 2743 is added in front of the client's first message.

The GSS-API OID is 1.3.6.1.5.5.16, with DER encoding 0x2b 0x06 0x01 0x05 0x05 0x10. Security contexts MUST set GSS_C_MUTUAL_FLAG to TRUE and MUST set GSS_C_DELEG_FLAG to FALSE, since credential delegation is not supported. Per-message tokens and GSS_Pseudo_random are not supported.

Mutual authentication depends on comparing the TLS server identity with the negotiated target name. The mechanism cannot do that itself because the application manages the TLS channel, so applications MUST match the TLS server identity with the target name as RFC 6125 describes. Acceptor names can use generic types such as GSS_C_NT_HOSTBASED_SERVICE, and the only initiator name type is GSS_C_NT_USER_NAME, so the identifier https://openid.example/ is its own user name value.
sections.plainLanguage: The same club entry trick also works for programs that use a different doorbell. They must still check they are at the right club door.

sections.title: An IMAP Example
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a user whose OpenID is https://openid.example logging in to an IMAP server at mail.example. The server lists AUTH=OPENID20 in its capabilities and the client sends the base64 of n,,https://openid.example/ as its initial response. The server replies with the base64 of an OpenID authentication request in which openid.mode is checkid_setup. No association is used in this example.

The client replies PQ==, the base64 of =, and passes the URL to a browser. The user logs in at the provider and agrees to authenticate, and the browser returns the result to the server. The server then sends SREG data for email and full name, the IMAP client answers with a blank response, and the server completes with OK. The transaction ID in the example is 1ef888c.
sections.plainLanguage: A mail program shows the club your card number, follows the link to the library desk, and waits. When the desk says yes, the club tells the program your name and lets it in.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The server is responsible for binding credentials to an authorization identity. A registration must therefore tie specific OpenIDs to specific identities in advance, or only specific trusted providers must be allowed with a predefined mapping. The example given is that https://example.com/user maps to user.

The initial client response can be abused. A malicious URL might add port numbers so the RP port scans a site, name an unauthorized or local host, or use a scheme such as file or ftp. Suggested mitigations: RPs keep a list of authorized URI bases, OPs SHOULD only redirect to RPs with the same domain component, RPs MUST NOT automatically retry failures, failures SHOULD be logged and client queries limited, and applications SHOULD NOT start browsers for providers they are not configured with.

On privacy, the OP learns each RP a user logs in to. Nothing in the protocol hides this, and nothing prohibits collecting it.
sections.plainLanguage: Be careful that nobody tricks the club into visiting strange places. Also, the library desk can see every club you join.

viz.caption: ABNF FOR THE FIRST AND LAST MESSAGES (RFC 6616 SECTIONS 3.1 AND 3.3)

data.title: Initial response and outcome data
data.code:
initial-response = gs2-header Auth-Identifier
Auth-Identifier = Identifier
Identifier = URI

outcome-data = [ sreg-avp *( "," sreg-avp ) ]
sreg-avp     = sreg-attr "=" sreg-val
sreg-attr    = sreg-word
sreg-val     = sreg-word
sreg-word    = 1*( unreserved / pct-encoded )
